Part 1
Your server.js, line by line
Code on the left. Predict the output first. Then click to reveal what the browser shows and what the server console prints.
server.js · the whole file
Five parts in one small file
// 1 · setup const express = require('express'); const fs = require('fs'); const server = express(); const data = fs.readFileSync('./index.html','utf-8'); // 2 · a middleware function const middleware1 = (req, res, next) => {   var login = true;   if (login) {     console.log("User has loggedIN......");     next();   } else {     res.send("Kindly Login");   } }; // 3 · application-level middleware server.use('/', middleware1);
// 4 · routes (API endpoints) server.get('/', (req, res) => {   res.send(data); }); server.get('/:id', (req, res) => {   res.send(`Testing...for id: ${req.params.id}`); }); server.post('/', (req, res) => {   res.send("Data posted"); }); server.put('/', (req, res) => {   res.send("Data updated"); }); // 5 · start listening server.listen(11000, () => {   console.log("Server running on port 11000"); });
Parts 1 & 5 · setup and listen
What happens on node server.js
server.js
const express = require('express'); // a function that builds an app const server = express(); // server has .use .get .post .put .listen const data = fs.readFileSync('./index.html',   'utf-8'); // runs ONCE, at startup → data is a string server.listen(11000, () => {   console.log("Server running on port 11000"); }); // opens port 11000 and waits for requests
GOOD TO KNOW
Edited index.html? Restart the server. The file was read once into data, not on every request.
No routes run yet. They run only when a request arrives.
SERVER CONSOLE
$ node server.js Server running on port 11000 ▌ (keeps running, waiting…)
Parts 2 & 3 · middleware1 with login = true
GET / passes the check, then reaches the route
server.js
const middleware1 = (req, res, next) => {   var login = true;   if (login) {     console.log("User has loggedIN......");     next(); // go on to the route   } else {     res.send("Kindly Login");   } }; server.use('/', middleware1); // every path server.get('/', (req, res) => {   res.send(data); });
localhost:11000
Welcome!
Your index.html, rendered as a page (because res.send(string) sends Content-Type text/html).
SERVER CONSOLE
Server running on port 11000 User has loggedIN...... User has loggedIN......
Twice? The browser also asked for /favicon.ico. Two slides ahead.
Parts 2 & 3 · middleware1 with login = false
The middleware answers, so no route runs
server.js
const middleware1 = (req, res, next) => {   var login = false; // changed   if (login) {     console.log("User has loggedIN......");     next();   } else {     res.send("Kindly Login"); // ends here   } }; server.use('/', middleware1); // none of these run now: // GET / GET /:id POST / PUT /
localhost:11000/42
Kindly Login
Same text for /, /42, /anything, and for POST and PUT too.
SERVER CONSOLE
Server running on port 11000 (nothing new: the log line is inside the if, which did not run)
Part 4 · a route parameter
:id catches whatever sits in that slot
server.js
server.get('/:id', (req, res) => {   console.log(req.params);   console.log(req.params.id);   console.log(typeof req.params.id);   console.log(req.ip);   res.send(`Testing...for id: ${req.params.id}`); }); // /42 → id = '42' // /about → id = 'about' // /a/b → no match (two segments)
localhost:11000/42
Testing...for id: 42
SERVER CONSOLE
User has loggedIN...... { id: '42' } 42 string ::1
::1 is “localhost” in IPv6. Params are always strings.
Gotcha · the hidden second request
You opened one page. The browser asked twice.
DEVTOOLS › NETWORK (F12)
Name
Status
Type
localhost
200
document
favicon.ico
200
text/html
The browser fetches /favicon.ico on its own to get the tab icon. That path has one segment, so it matches '/:id' with id = 'favicon.ico'.
SERVER CONSOLE
User has loggedIN...... User has loggedIN...... { id: 'favicon.ico' }
ONE FIX: ANSWER IT FIRST
server.get('/favicon.ico',   (req, res) => res.sendStatus(204)); // put it ABOVE '/:id'
Routes are checked top to bottom. First match wins.

Part 2
req: what the request carries
Every piece of the URL, every header, the caller’s address and the body, already parsed for you by Express.
Anatomy of one request
Express splits the URL into labelled pieces
route: server.get('/products/:id', handler)
req.method 'GET'
req.params.id '7'
http://localhost:11000/products/7?sort=desc&limit=3
req.protocol 'http'
req.hostname 'localhost'
req.path '/products/7'
req.query { sort: 'desc', limit: '3' }
req.originalUrl → '/products/7?sort=desc&limit=3'
req.get('host') → 'localhost:11000'
Every value is a string, even '7' and '3'.
req · method, url, path
Log it all, then send it back as JSON
server.js
server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   console.log('method ', req.method);   console.log('url ', req.url);   console.log('originalUrl', req.originalUrl);   console.log('path ', req.path);   console.log('hostname ', req.hostname);   console.log('protocol ', req.protocol);   res.json({     method: req.method,     path: req.path   }); });
localhost:11000/products/7?sort=desc
{"method":"GET",  "path":"/products/7"}
SERVER CONSOLE
method GET url /products/7?sort=desc originalUrl /products/7?sort=desc path /products/7 hostname localhost protocol http
req.params · more than one
Each :name in the route becomes a key
server.js
server.get(   '/products/:id/reviews/:reviewId',   (req, res) => {     console.log(req.params);     console.log(req.params.id + 1);     const id = Number(req.params.id);     console.log(id + 1);     res.json(req.params);   } );
localhost:11000/products/7/reviews/3
{"id":"7","reviewId":"3"}
SERVER CONSOLE
{ id: '7', reviewId: '3' } 71 8
'7' + 1 joins text. Convert with Number() before doing maths or comparing with ===.
req.query · everything after ?
Optional filters, no route change needed
server.js
server.get('/products', (req, res) => {   console.log(req.query);   const { category, limit } = req.query;   console.log(category, limit, typeof limit);   console.log(req.query.sort); // not sent   res.send(     `category=${category}, limit=${limit}`   ); }); // params → which thing (/products/7) // query → how to filter it (?limit=2)
…/products?category=jewelery&limit=2
category=jewelery, limit=2
SERVER CONSOLE
{ category: 'jewelery', limit: '2' } jewelery 2 string undefined
Missing keys are undefined, not errors. Values are strings again.
req.headers, req.get(), req.ip
Who is asking, and from where
server.js
server.get('/whoami', (req, res) => {   console.log(req.ip);   console.log(req.get('User-Agent'));   console.log(req.headers.host);   console.log(req.headers['accept-language']);   console.log(req.secure);   res.json({     ip: req.ip,     browser: req.get('User-Agent')   }); }); // req.get() ignores case; req.headers keys // are always lowercase
localhost:11000/whoami
{"ip":"::1","browser":"Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 …"}
SERVER CONSOLE
::1 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; … localhost:11000 en-IN,en;q=0.9 false
Open it from a phone on the same Wi-Fi and req.ip changes.
req.body · data sent with POST or PUT
req.body is empty until something reads it
server.js
server.use(express.json()); // ↑ this one line fills req.body server.post('/products', (req, res) => {   console.log(req.body);   console.log(req.body.title, req.body.price);   res.status(201).json({     id: 21,     ...req.body   }); });
POST
localhost:11000/products
Body (JSON): {"title":"Steel Bottle","price":12.5}
Status: 201 Created
{"id":21,"title":"Steel Bottle","price":12.5}
SERVER CONSOLE
{ title: 'Steel Bottle', price: 12.5 } Steel Bottle 12.5
Remove express.json() and req.body is undefined, so req.body.title throws a TypeError.
Cheat sheet · req
GET /products/7?sort=desc on route /products/:id
Property
Value
req.method
'GET'
req.params
{ id: '7' }
req.query
{ sort: 'desc' }
req.path
'/products/7'
req.originalUrl
'/products/7?sort=desc'
req.hostname
'localhost'
req.protocol
'http'
Property
Value
req.ip
'::1'
req.get('User-Agent')
'Mozilla/5.0 …'
req.headers
all headers, lowercase keys
req.baseUrl
'' (or '/api' inside a router)
req.url
prefix removed inside a router
req.body
undefined until express.json()
req.cookies
undefined until cookie-parser
Rule of thumb: URL pieces are always strings; only a parsed JSON body keeps numbers and booleans.
Part 3
res: everything you can send back
Text, HTML, JSON, files, downloads, redirects, status codes, headers and cookies. One answer per request.
The one rule of res
Answer exactly once. Use return to stop.
server.js · a very common bug
server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   const p = products.find(     x => x.id === Number(req.params.id));   if (!p) {     res.status(404).send('Not found');     // no return → code keeps going   }   res.json(p); // second answer! }); // fix: if (!p) return res.status(404).send('Not found');
localhost:11000/products/99
Not found
The browser got the first answer. The second one crashed on the server.
SERVER CONSOLE
Error [ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT]: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client
at ServerResponse.setHeader …
res.send() · predict, then click
send() looks at what you give it
You write
Browser shows
Content-Type
res.send('Hello')
Hello
text/html
res.send('<h1>Hi</h1>')
Hi, as a big heading
text/html
res.send({ id: 1 })
{"id":1}
application/json
res.send([1, 2])
[1,2]
application/json
res.send(Buffer.from('hi'))
a file download
application/octet-stream
What will the browser show?
String → HTML
Your teacher-code index.html renders because of this.
Object or array → JSON
send() hands it to res.json() for you.
res.json(), res.status(), res.sendStatus()
Data plus a status code that tells the truth
server.js
server.get('/api/products/:id', (req, res) => {   const p = products.find(     x => x.id === Number(req.params.id));   if (!p) {     return res.status(404)       .json({ error: 'Product not found' });   }   res.json(p); // status 200 by default }); server.delete('/api/products/:id',   (req, res) => res.sendStatus(204)); // status() alone sends nothing: chain it!
localhost:11000/api/products/99
{"error":"Product not found"}
Network tab: 404 Not Found
STATUS CODES YOU WILL USE
200 OK
201 Created
204 No Content
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
404 Not Found
500 Server Error
302 Redirect
sendStatus(401) sends the word “Unauthorized” as the body.
res.sendFile()
Send a file without reading it yourself
server.js
// before: read once, send the string // const data = fs.readFileSync(...) const path = require('path'); server.get('/', (req, res) => {   res.sendFile(path.join(__dirname, 'index.html')); }); // ✗ relative path res.sendFile('index.html'); // ✓ or give a root res.sendFile('index.html', { root: __dirname });
WHY IT’S BETTER
Reads the file on each request, so edits show on refresh.
Sets Content-Type from the extension: .html, .png, .pdf.
SERVER CONSOLE · THE ✗ LINE
TypeError: path must be absolute or specify root to res.sendFile
__dirname is the folder that holds server.js.
res.redirect() and res.download()
Send the browser elsewhere, or save a file
server.js
server.get('/shop', (req, res) => {   res.redirect('/products'); // 302 }); server.get('/old-products', (req, res) => {   res.redirect(301, '/products'); // moved }); server.get('/products/:id/image', (req, res) => {   const p = findProduct(req.params.id);   res.redirect(p.image); // another site }); server.get('/invoice', (req, res) => {   res.download(path.join(__dirname, 'invoice.pdf')); });
/shop → localhost:11000/products
You typed /shop. The address bar now says /products: the browser made a second request on its own.
DEVTOOLS › NETWORK
Name
Status
Note
shop
302
Location
products
200
page
invoice

res.set(), res.type(), res.cookie(), res.end()
Labels on the envelope, before you seal it
server.js
server.get('/api/products', (req, res) => {   res.set('X-Total-Count', String(products.length));   res.set('Cache-Control', 'no-store');   res.cookie('lastVisit', 'products');   res.json(products); }); server.get('/plain', (req, res) => {   res.type('text').send('<h1>not rendered</h1>'); }); server.get('/logout', (req, res) => {   res.clearCookie('lastVisit').end(); });
RESPONSE HEADERS · /api/products
HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-Powered-By: Express X-Total-Count: 20 Cache-Control: no-store Set-Cookie: lastVisit=products; Path=/ Content-Type: application/json
localhost:11000/plain
<h1>not rendered</h1>
text/plain: the tags show as text.
Cheat sheet · res
Prepare as much as you like, finish once
Finishes the response (pick one)
Method
Sends
res.send(x)
text, HTML or JSON
res.json(obj)
JSON
res.sendStatus(404)
code + “Not Found”
res.sendFile(absPath)
a file to view
res.download(path)
a file to save
res.redirect('/x')
302 + Location
res.end()
nothing more
res.render(view)
HTML from a template
Prepares it (chain, then finish)
Method
Sets
res.status(201)
status code
res.set(name, val)
any header
res.type('json')
Content-Type
res.cookie(name, val)
Set-Cookie
res.clearCookie(name)
expires a cookie
res.locals.x = …
data for this request
Heads-up · Express 5
Old tutorials show v4 code. Spot the difference.
Seen in old (v4) tutorials
Write this in Express 5
res.send(404)
res.sendStatus(404)
res.json(obj, 404)
res.status(404).json(obj)
res.redirect('back')
res.redirect(req.get('Referrer') || '/')
req.body is {} with no parser
req.body is undefined with no parser
app.get('*', …)
app.get('/*splat', …), or a final app.use for 404s
async errors need try/catch
a rejected promise reaches the error handler by itself
npm install express now installs version 5. Check yours with npm ls express.

Setup · get the 20 products into your server
Two ways to load the data
A · Save a file (best for class)

Set 1 · req.params, res.json, res.status · level 1
Find one product by id
BUILD
  1. GET /products/:id → the product as JSON
  2. Unknown id → status 404 and an error object
  3. GET /products/:id/price → only id and price
  4. GET /products/:id/rating → only the rating
  5. Bonus: id that is not a number → 400
EXPECTED OUTPUT
/products/5 {"id":5,"title":"John Hardy Women's…","price":695,…} /products/99 404 {"error":"Product 99 not found"} /products/5/price {"id":5,"price":695} /products/11/rating {"rate":4.8,"count":319} /products/abc 400 {"error":"id must be a number"}
Hint: Number(req.params.id), then products.find(p => p.id === id). Check Number.isNaN(id) for the bonus.
Set 2 · req.query, res.set · level 2
One route, many filters
BUILD · GET /products
  1. ?category=… keeps one category
  2. ?maxPrice=… keeps price ≤ that number
  3. ?sort=desc reverses the order
  4. ?limit=… keeps the first n
  5. Any mix of them works together
  6. Header X-Total-Count = items returned
Request (/products…)
ids returned
?category=electronics
9–14 (6)
?maxPrice=20
4, 7, 8, 18, 19, 20
?limit=3
1, 2, 3
?sort=desc&limit=3
20, 19, 18
?category=jewelery&maxPrice=50
7, 8
?category=toys
[] (0)
Hint: start with let list = [...products], filter step by step, apply limit last. Query values are strings: Number(maxPrice).

Set 5 · req.body, POST, PUT, DELETE · level 3
Change the data, not just read it
BUILD (use Thunder Client)
  1. Add server.use(express.json())
  2. POST /products → new id = highest id + 1, push it, reply 201
  3. No title, or price not a number → 400
  4. PUT /products/:id → update only the fields sent
  5. DELETE /products/:id → 204, then GET gives 404
EXPECTED OUTPUT
POST /products {"title":"Steel Bottle","price":12.5} 201 {"id":21,"title":"Steel Bottle","price":12.5} POST /products {"price":"cheap"} 400 {"error":"title and price are required"} PUT /products/21 {"price":9.99} 200 {"id":21,"title":"Steel Bottle","price":9.99} DELETE /products/21 204 (empty body) GET /products/21 404 {"error":"Product 21 not found"}
Hint: Object.assign(product, req.body) for PUT; products.splice(index, 1) for DELETE. Restart the server and all changes vanish: data lives in memory.

Think like an API designer

Last row: put server.use((req, res) => …) after every route. It runs only when nothing matched.
That function is your first hand-written middleware. Keep it. We start the next part with it.
Reference solution · sets 1 and 2
Compare with yours after you try
Set 1 · one product
server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   const id = Number(req.params.id);   if (Number.isNaN(id)) {     return res.status(400)       .json({ error: 'id must be a number' });   }   const p = products.find(x => x.id === id);   if (!p) {     return res.status(404)       .json({ error: `Product ${id} not found` });   }   res.json(p); });
Set 2 · filters
server.get('/products', (req, res) => {   const q = req.query;   let list = [...products];   if (q.category) list = list.filter(     p => p.category === q.category);   if (q.maxPrice) list = list.filter(     p => p.price <= Number(q.maxPrice));   if (q.sort === 'desc') list.reverse();   if (q.limit)     list = list.slice(0, Number(q.limit));   res.set('X-Total-Count', String(list.length));   res.json(list); });
Quiz · req & res · 1 of 8 · MCQ: one answer
Route is /products/:id. The request is /products/7?sort=desc. What is req.params.id?
A 7 (a number)
B '7' (a string)
C '7?sort=desc'
D undefined
Answer: B
Route params are always strings, and the query string is never part of a param.
Quiz · req & res · 2 of 8 · MCQ: one answer
Same request, /products/7?sort=desc. What is req.query?
A { sort: 'desc' }
B 'sort=desc'
C { id: '7', sort: 'desc' }
D undefined
Answer: A
Express parses the query string into an object. The id lives in req.params, not req.query.
Quiz · req & res · 3 of 8 · MSQ: choose all that apply
Express 5. A client POSTs JSON to /products, but the app never calls express.json(). Which are true?
A req.body is undefined
B req.body is an empty object {}
C req.body.title throws a TypeError
D Adding express.json() above the route fixes it
E Adding express.json() below the route fixes it
Answer: A, C, D
In Express 5 req.body stays undefined without a parser. Middleware below the route runs too late.
Quiz · req & res · 4 of 8 · MCQ: one answer
res.send({ id: 1 }) sets which Content-Type?
A text/html
B text/plain
C application/json
D none, you must set it
Answer: C
Objects and arrays are handed to res.json(). Strings get text/html.
Quiz · req & res · 5 of 8 · MSQ: choose all that apply
Which calls finish the response, so the browser stops waiting?
A res.json(p)
B res.status(404)
C res.sendStatus(404)
D res.set('X-A', '1')
E res.redirect('/')
Answer: A, C, E
status() and set() only prepare the response. Alone, they leave the browser spinning.
Quiz · req & res · 6 of 8 · MCQ: one answer
Our class server.js, login = true. You open localhost:11000/about. What appears?
A 404 Cannot GET /about
B Testing...for id: about
C Kindly Login
D The index.html page
Answer: B
“about” is one path segment, so '/:id' matches it. The middleware logged first, then called next().
Quiz · req & res · 7 of 8 · MCQ: one answer
What happens on GET /x?
server.get('/x', (req, res) => {   res.send('one');   res.send('two'); });
A Browser shows two
B Browser shows onetwo
C Shows one; server logs ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT
D Nothing is sent at all
Answer: C
The first send() finished the response. The second one throws on the server.
Quiz · req & res · 8 of 8 · MSQ: choose all that apply
Routes in this order. Which statements are true?
server.get('/products/:id', getOne); server.get('/products/categories', listCategories); server.get('/products/category/:name', byCategory);
A /products/categories runs getOne
B /products/categories runs listCategories
C /products/category/jewelery runs byCategory
D /products/category runs getOne
Answer: A, C, D
:id grabs any single segment, including the words “categories” and “category”. First match wins.
Part 5
Middleware: the code between req and res
You have already written two: middleware1 and the 404 catch-all. Now we see why they exist, and the five kinds Express gives you.
The problem · no middleware
Log every request, check login on every route
server.get('/products', (req, res) => {   console.log(new Date().toISOString(), req.method, req.url);   if (req.query.token !== 'abc123') return res.status(401).send('Kindly Login');   res.json(products); }); server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   console.log(new Date().toISOString(), req.method, req.url);   if (req.query.token !== 'abc123') return res.status(401).send('Kindly Login');   res.json(findProduct(req.params.id)); }); server.post('/products', (req, res) => {   console.log(new Date().toISOString(), req.method, req.url);   if (req.query.token !== 'abc123') return res.status(401).send('Kindly Login');   res.status(201).json(addProduct(req.body)); }); // …and 17 more routes
40 copies
of the same 2 lines across 20 routes
20 edits
when the token rule changes
1 forgotten
copy is an unprotected route nobody notices
Definition
A middleware is a function with a third argument
(req, res, next) => { … }
the request · the response · “pass it on” button
Run any code
log, time, count, check
Change req, res
add req.user, req.body, a header
End the cycle
answer early: 401, 404, 500
Call next()
hand over to the next one
If it doesn’t end the cycle, it must call next(). Otherwise the request is left hanging.
Watch it run
Each function passes the request on, or answers
Step 1 · a logger
Write it once, it runs for every request
server.js
// the guide’s version: // console.log('Time:', Date.now()) server.use((req, res, next) => {   const time = new Date().toISOString();   console.log(time, req.method, req.url);   next(); }); server.get('/products', (req, res) =>   res.json(products)); server.get('/products/:id', getOne); // no path → runs for every request
YOU OPEN, IN ORDER
/products /products/5 /nope (404)
SERVER CONSOLE
2026-10-26T05:12:01.118Z GET /products 2026-10-26T05:12:05.430Z GET /products/5 2026-10-26T05:12:09.902Z GET /nope
Even /nope is logged: the logger runs before Express knows no route matches.
Step 2 · forget next()
No next(), no answer: the browser waits forever
server.js
server.use((req, res, next) => {   console.log(req.method, req.url);   // next(); ← forgotten }); server.get('/products', (req, res) =>   res.json(products)); // never reached // every middleware must do ONE of: // next() → pass it on // res.send(...) → answer it
SERVER CONSOLE
GET /products
No error, no crash. Just silence. That is what makes this bug hard to spot.
Step 3 · order matters
Registered after the route? Too late.
server.js
server.get('/products', (req, res) =>   res.json(products)); // logger registered AFTER the route server.use((req, res, next) => {   console.log(req.method, req.url);   next(); });
YOU OPEN
/products → list shown /nope → 404
Express walks the list top to bottom and stops at the first function that answers.
SERVER CONSOLE
GET /nope
/products is missing: the route answered first. /nope reached the logger only because no route matched it.
Rule: things that should run for everything go at the top. 404 and error handlers go at the bottom.
Step 4 · add things to req
Middleware can leave notes for the route
server.js
server.use((req, res, next) => {   req.requestTime = Date.now();   next(); }); server.use('/products', (req, res, next) => {   res.locals.store = 'Fake Store';   next(); }); server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   res.json({     title: findProduct(req.params.id).title,     store: res.locals.store,     tookMs: Date.now() - req.requestTime   }); });
localhost:11000/products/3
{"title":"Mens Cotton Jacket",  "store":"Fake Store",  "tookMs":1}
YOU’VE SEEN THIS BEFORE
express.json() is a middleware that fills req.body.
cookie-parser fills req.cookies. An auth check can fill req.user.
Step 5 · the fix · middleware1, done properly
40 copies become 2 lines
server.js
const checkLogin = (req, res, next) => {   if (req.query.token === 'abc123') {     console.log("User has loggedIN......");     return next();   }   res.status(401).send("Kindly Login"); }; server.use(logger); server.use(checkLogin); server.get('/products', listAll); server.get('/products/:id', getOne); server.post('/products', addOne);
BROWSER
/products
401 · Kindly Login
/products?token=abc123
[{"id":1,"title":"Fjallraven…
SERVER CONSOLE
… GET /products … GET /products?token=abc123 User has loggedIN......
Change the token rule once; every route follows.
Type 1 · application-level · with a mount path
app.use(path, fn) runs only under that path
server.js · from the Express guide
// no path: every request server.use((req, res, next) => {   console.log('Time:', Date.now());   next(); }); // with a path: any METHOD on /products/:id server.use('/products/:id', (req, res, next) => {   console.log('Request Type:', req.method);   next(); });
DOES THE SECOND ONE RUN?
Request
Runs?
GET /products/5
yes
DELETE /products/5
yes
GET /products/5/reviews
yes (prefix)
GET /products
no
CONSOLE · DELETE /products/5
Time: 1793006021118 Request Type: DELETE
Type 1 · app.use vs app.METHOD
Same path, very different reach
Request
app.use('/products', fn)
app.get('/products', fn)
GET /products
runs
runs
POST /products
runs
no (GET only)
GET /products/5
runs (prefix)
no (exact path)
GET /productsXYZ
no
no
usual job
prepare, then next()
answer the request
next('route')
not available
available
INSIDE app.use('/products', …) FOR GET /products/5
req.originalUrl '/products/5' req.baseUrl '/products' req.url '/5'
Type 1 · middleware sub-stack
Several functions in one call, run left to right
server.js · from the Express guide
server.use(   '/products/:id',   (req, res, next) => { // 1st     console.log('Request URL:', req.originalUrl);     next();   },   (req, res, next) => { // 2nd     console.log('Request Type:', req.method);     next();   } ); server.get('/products/:id', getOne); // 3rd
localhost:11000/products/2?ref=ad
{"id":2,"title":"Mens Casual Premium Slim Fit T-Shirts ",…}
SERVER CONSOLE
Request URL: /products/2?ref=ad Request Type: GET
Each next() hands over to the function to its right, then to the next registered one.
Type 1 · multiple route handlers
Two routes for one path: the second never runs
server.js · from the Express guide
server.get(   '/products/:id',   (req, res, next) => {     console.log('ID:', req.params.id);     next();   },   (req, res) => {     res.send('Product Info'); // ends it   } ); // same path, registered later server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   res.send(req.params.id); // never called });
localhost:11000/products/5
Product Info
Not “5”: the first route already answered.
SERVER CONSOLE
ID: 5
No error either. A duplicate route is silently dead code, so keep one route per path and method.
Type 1 · next('route')
Skip the rest of this route, try the next one
server.js · from the Express guide
server.get(   '/products/:id',   (req, res, next) => {     if (req.params.id === '0') next('route');     else next();   },   (req, res) => {     res.send('regular');   } ); server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   res.send('special'); });
BROWSER
You open
You see
/products/5
regular
/products/0
special
next() → the next function in this route. next('route') → jump to the next matching route.
ONLY WORKS IN
app.get / post / put / delete and router.get / post / …, never in app.use().
Type 1 · reusable middleware arrays
Name your middleware, group it, reuse it
server.js · from the Express guide
function logOriginalUrl(req, res, next) {   console.log('Request URL:', req.originalUrl);   next(); } function logMethod(req, res, next) {   console.log('Request Type:', req.method);   next(); } const logStuff = [logOriginalUrl, logMethod]; server.get('/products/:id', logStuff, getOne); server.delete('/products/:id', logStuff, checkLogin, removeOne);
CONSOLE · DELETE /products/5?token=abc123
Request URL: /products/5?token=abc123 Request Type: DELETE User has loggedIN......
WHY IT HELPS
Arrays and single functions can be mixed freely. Express flattens them into one chain, in the order written.
Type 2 · router-level · first, WITHOUT Router
The store grows: public products, private admin
app.js · everything in one file
app.get('/api/products', listAll); app.get('/api/products/categories', listCategories); app.get('/api/products/:id', getOne); app.get('/api/admin/stats', checkAdmin, stats); app.post('/api/admin/products', checkAdmin, addOne); app.put('/api/admin/products/:id', checkAdmin, updateOne); app.delete('/api/admin/products/:id', checkAdmin, removeOne); // + orders, users, carts, reviews… // app.js becomes a 300-line list
Prefix typed 7 times
Rename /api to /api/v2? Edit every line.
checkAdmin on each line
The next admin route someone adds may forget it.
No “admin” unit
You can move the handler functions to other files, but the paths and checks stay in app.js.
Type 2 · why the guide’s Router example confuses
Same code, app. swapped for router.
Application-level (no Router)
const app = express(); app.use((req, res, next) => {   console.log('Time:', Date.now());   next(); }); app.use('/user/:id', logUrl, logType); app.get('/user/:id', checkZero, regular); app.get('/user/:id', special);
Router-level (the guide’s version)
const app = express(); const router = express.Router(); router.use((req, res, next) => {   console.log('Time:', Date.now());   next(); }); router.use('/user/:id', logUrl, logType); router.get('/user/:id', checkZero, regular); router.get('/user/:id', special); app.use('/', router);
Identical output. Mounted at '/' in one file, Router adds nothing yet.
Its value shows up when you mount it at a prefix, move it to its own file, and give it its own middleware.
Type 2 · router-level · now WITH Router
Each group becomes a mini-app in its own file
routes/products.js
const express = require('express'); const router = express.Router(); router.get('/', listAll); router.get('/categories', listCategories); router.get('/:id', getOne); module.exports = router;
routes/admin.js
const router = require('express').Router(); router.use(checkAdmin); // once, for all router.get('/stats', stats); router.post('/products', addOne); router.put('/products/:id', updateOne); router.delete('/products/:id', removeOne); module.exports = router;
app.js · the whole routing table
const products = require('./routes/products'); const admin = require('./routes/admin'); app.use('/api/products', products); app.use('/api/admin', admin);
Prefix in one place. Paths inside are relative.
Check in one place. New admin routes are protected automatically.
No app passed around. Each file exports a unit.
Watch it route
app.js picks the router; the router picks the route
Type 2 · router.use() is scoped
checkAdmin guards admin, and only admin
middleware/checkAdmin.js
function checkAdmin(req, res, next) {   if (req.query.token !== 'admin') {     return res.sendStatus(401);   }   console.log('baseUrl', req.baseUrl);   console.log('url ', req.url);   console.log('orig ', req.originalUrl);   next(); } module.exports = checkAdmin;
BROWSER
You open
Result
/api/products
200 list
/api/products/5
200 one
/api/admin/stats
Unauthorized
…/stats?token=admin
200 stats
CONSOLE · LAST REQUEST
baseUrl /api/admin url /stats?token=admin orig /api/admin/stats?token=admin
Type 2 · next('router')
Leave the whole router at once
With Router · from the Express guide
const router = express.Router(); router.use((req, res, next) => {   if (!req.headers['x-auth']) return next('router');   next(); }); router.get('/user/:id', (req, res) => {   res.send('hello, user!'); }); app.use('/admin', router, (req, res) => {   res.sendStatus(401); // anything that fell out });
Same result, without Router
app.get('/admin/user/:id', (req, res) => {   if (!req.headers['x-auth']) {     return res.sendStatus(401);   }   res.send('hello, user!'); }); // fine for 1 route; repeat for 20?
TERMINAL
$ curl localhost:11000/admin/user/7 Unauthorized $ curl -H "x-auth: 1" localhost:11000/admin/user/7 hello, user!
Type 3 · error-handling · the problem
Throw an error and Express answers for you
server.js · no error handler yet
server.get('/products/:id', (req, res) => {   const p = findProduct(req.params.id);   if (!p) {     throw new Error('Product not found');   }   res.json(p); }); // Express catches it and uses its own // built-in error handler
localhost:11000/products/99
Error: Product not found     at /home/you/store/server.js:14:11     at Layer.handle …
Status 500 · your file paths, shown to anyone
SERVER CONSOLE
Error: Product not found     at /home/you/store/server.js:14:11     at Layer.handle …
The server keeps running. The client just gets an ugly HTML page and the wrong status (should be 404).
Type 3 · your own error handler
Four arguments: (err, req, res, next)
server.js
server.get('/products/:id', (req, res, next) => {   const p = findProduct(req.params.id);   if (!p) {     const err = new Error('Product not found');     err.status = 404;     return next(err); // ← jump to the handler   }   res.json(p); }); // LAST, after every route server.use((err, req, res, next) => {   console.error('Handled:', err.message);   res.status(err.status || 500)     .json({ error: err.message }); });
localhost:11000/products/99
{"error":"Product not found"}
Status 404 · clean JSON, no stack trace
SERVER CONSOLE
Handled: Product not found
Keep all four parameters, even if you never use next. Express counts them to know this is an error handler.
Watch errors travel
An error skips everything until a 4-argument function
Type 3 · async errors and the 404 handler
Express 5 catches async errors for you
server.js · end of the file
const API = 'https://fakestoreapi.com/products/'; server.get('/live/:id', async (req, res) => {   const r = await fetch(API + req.params.id);   res.json(await r.json()); }); // no try/catch needed in v5 // 404: normal middleware, near the end server.use((req, res) => {   res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' }); }); // errors: 4 params, the very last server.use((err, req, res, next) => {   console.error('Handled:', err.message);   res.status(err.status || 500)     .json({ error: err.message }); });
TRY IT: WI-FI OFF, OPEN /live/3
Handled: fetch failed
Browser: 500 {"error":"fetch failed"}
TWO TRAPS
(err, req, res) with 3 params is not an error handler. Errors pass straight by it.
Express 4 tutorials wrap every async route in try/catch + next(err). In v5 a rejected promise goes to the handler by itself.
Type 4 · built-in · express.json and express.urlencoded
Two body readers, one for each kind of client
server.js
// JSON: fetch(), Thunder Client, Postman server.use(express.json()); // HTML <form> posts server.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: false })); server.post('/products', (req, res) => {   const { title, price } = req.body;   console.log(title, price, typeof price);   res.send(`Added ${title}`); });
BROWSER · public/add.html
Steel Bottle
12.5
Add
After clicking Add, the page shows:
Added Steel Bottle
SERVER CONSOLE
form: Steel Bottle 12.5 string JSON: Steel Bottle 12.5 number
Forms always send text. JSON keeps numbers. Also built in: express.text() and express.raw().
Type 4 · built-in · express.static
One line serves a whole folder
server.js · the class code, upgraded
// const fs = require('fs'); // const data = fs.readFileSync(...); // server.get('/', (req,res) => res.send(data)); const path = require('path'); server.use(express.static(   path.join(__dirname, 'public') )); // store/ // server.js // public/index.html style.css logo.png
WHAT EACH URL GETS
URL
Answer
/
public/index.html
/style.css
text/css file
/logo.png
image/png file
/products
no file: next() → route
No file found? It calls next(), so your routes still work. That is middleware behaviour.
Edit index.html, refresh: the change shows. No restart.
Type 5 · third-party · cookie-parser (the guide’s example)
npm install, require, app.use. Done.
$ npm install cookie-parser
const cookieParser = require('cookie-parser'); server.use(cookieParser()); // fills req.cookies server.get('/theme/:name', (req, res) => {   res.cookie('theme', req.params.name);   res.send(`Theme set to ${req.params.name}`); }); server.get('/products', (req, res) => {   console.log(req.cookies.theme);   res.json({     theme: req.cookies.theme || 'light',     count: products.length   }); });
BROWSER, IN ORDER
/products
{"theme":"light","count":20}
/theme/dark → Theme set to dark
/products
{"theme":"dark","count":20}
SERVER CONSOLE
undefined dark
Remove cookieParser() and req.cookies is undefined: the same story as req.body.
Type 5 · third-party · morgan and cors
Others already wrote the middleware you need
$ npm install morgan cors
const morgan = require('morgan'); const cors = require('cors'); server.use(morgan('dev')); // replaces our logger server.use(cors()); // let other sites call us
Package
Adds
morgan
request logging
cors
cross-origin headers
cookie-parser
req.cookies
multer
file uploads (req.file)
express-session
login sessions (req.session)
compression
gzip responses
SERVER CONSOLE · morgan('dev')
GET /products/5 200 2.871 ms - 453 GET /nope 404 0.904 ms - 21 GET /products/99 404 1.233 ms - 29
method · path · status · time · bytes sent
RESPONSE HEADER ADDED BY cors()
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Without it, a React app on localhost:5173 calling your API on :11000 is blocked by the browser.
Everything together · app.js
All five types, in the order they must run
const express = require('express'); const morgan = require('morgan'); const products = require('./routes/products'); const admin = require('./routes/admin'); const app = express(); app.use(morgan('dev')); // 5 third-party app.use(express.json()); // 4 built-in app.use(express.static('public')); // 4 built-in app.use((req, res, next) => { // 1 application-level   req.requestTime = Date.now(); next(); }); app.use('/api/products', products); // 2 router-level app.use('/api/admin', admin); // 2 (checkAdmin inside) app.use((req, res) => // 404: normal middleware   res.status(404).json({ error: 'Not found' })); app.use((err, req, res, next) => // 3 error-handling   res.status(err.status || 500).json({ error: err.message })); app.listen(11000);
1 · log every request
2 · read bodies, serve files
3 · stamp req for later
4 · hand to a router
5 · nothing matched → 404
6 · something broke → error
Four requests through the full pipeline
Each one stops at a different place
Cheat sheet · the five types
Where it’s attached decides where it runs
Type
Written as
Use it for
Application-level
app.use(fn), app.get(path, fn)
logging, auth or stamps for the whole app
Router-level
router.use(fn), router.get(…)
one feature under one prefix, in its own file
Error-handling
(err, req, res, next) => …
one place that formats every error
Built-in
express.json(), .urlencoded(), .static()
reading bodies, serving files
Third-party
npm i morgan → app.use(morgan('dev'))
logging, cors, cookies, uploads, sessions
next() or respond
never neither, never both
Order = run order
general on top, safety nets last
4 params = error
keep next even if unused
404 is not an error
it’s the last normal one
Quiz · middleware · 1 of 7 · MCQ: one answer
GET /products with this as the first middleware. What does the browser do?
app.use((req, res, next) => {   console.log(req.method, req.url); });
A Shows 404 Cannot GET
B Shows a 500 error
C Keeps loading, no answer
D Shows the products list
Answer: C
It neither calls next() nor sends a response, so the request is left hanging.
Quiz · middleware · 2 of 7 · MCQ: one answer
Which function will Express use as an error handler?
A (req, res, next) => …
B (err, req, res) => …
C (err, req, res, next) => …
D (error) => …
Answer: C
Express counts the parameters. Exactly four means “error handler”, even if next is never used.
Quiz · middleware · 3 of 7 · MSQ: choose all that apply
Which come built into Express, with no npm install?
A express.json()
B cors()
C express.static()
D express.urlencoded()
E morgan('dev')
Answer: A, C, D
Built-ins hang off express itself. cors and morgan are third-party packages from npm.
Quiz · middleware · 4 of 7 · MCQ: one answer
Given this line, which request does NOT run mw?
app.use('/products', mw);
A GET /products
B POST /products
C GET /products/7/reviews
D GET /product
Answer: D
app.use matches any method and anything under /products. /product is a different path.
Quiz · middleware · 5 of 7 · MCQ: one answer
GET /products. Does the logger print anything?
app.get('/products', (req, res) => res.json(products)); app.use(logger); // logs, then next()
A Yes, before the route runs
B Yes, after the route runs
C No, the route already answered
D It throws an error
Answer: C
Registration order is run order. The route ended the cycle, so Express never reached the logger.
Quiz · middleware · 6 of 7 · MSQ: choose all that apply
Good reasons to use express.Router()?
A Write a group’s prefix once, in app.js
B Attach middleware to just that group
C Move a feature to its own file without passing app
D It makes requests run faster
E next('route') only works with a router
Answer: A, B, C
Router is about organisation, not speed. next('route') also works with app.get / app.post.
Quiz · middleware · 7 of 7 · MCQ: one answer
Express 5, no try/catch. The fetch fails. What happens?
app.get('/live/:id', async (req, res) => {   const r = await fetch(API + req.params.id);   res.json(await r.json()); });
A The whole server crashes
B The request hangs forever
C The error handler receives it
D Express sends 200 with no body
Answer: C
Express 5 forwards a rejected promise to the error handler, the same as next(err).
What to remember
req brings it in. res sends it out. Middleware sits between.
req offers
params · query body · cookies headers · get() method · path · ip
URL parts are strings. Body and cookies need middleware.
res sends
send · json status().json() sendStatus · sendFile redirect · download
Exactly once per request. Use return to stop early.
middleware helps
Write once, run everywhere: logging, login checks, body parsing, static files, 404s and errors.
next() or respond. Order matters. Router groups it.
